item.title: Calling Rust From PHP Without a Socket, Part 2: Making Existing Code Use It
item.description: Part 1 covered the plumbing: ePHPm registers ephpm_kv_* and ephpm_db_* functions that call straight into Rust, and a cache read through one costs about a tenth of a microsecond instead of a loopback round trip. That’s nice and also useless on its own, because nobody is going to rewrite their WordPress object cache or their Laravel cache store around a function called ephpm_kv_set(). Applications talk to Redis through phpredis or Predis, to the cache through PSR-6/16 or wp_cache_*, and to the database through wpdb, mysqli, Eloquent or DBAL.

item.title: Zero-Dependency Deployments - Single Binary for WordPress
item.description: The standard way to run a WordPress site is four services: nginx for HTTP and TLS, php-fpm to run PHP, MySQL for data, and Redis once the site gets slow enough that someone installs an object cache plugin. That’s four processes, four config files, three sockets between them, and four things to upgrade. For a big site that’s fine. For a brochure site, a staging copy, a PR preview, a CI job that needs a real WordPress to test a plugin against, or a box at the edge, it’s absurd.

item.title: What Does One More WordPress Site Cost?
item.description: ePHPm v0.7.0 shipped per-site multi-tenancy: point [server] sites_dir at a directory, every Host maps to its own docroot and its own Turso database file, and one process serves all of them. The first question anybody asks about that is “how many sites fit on a box?”, and the honest way to answer it is to turn the question around. What does one more site cost? If you know the marginal RAM, file descriptors, CPU and disk for a tenant, the box size falls out of arithmetic.

item.title: Faking MySQL's Quirks Well Enough to Fool WordPress
item.description: Last month I wrote about running SQLite behind a MySQL socket with litewire, and ended on “passing an install suite is not the same thing as behaving like MySQL”. That turned out to be accurate. On August 10th a few things happened at once: I put a real WordPress 7.0.3 site through a benchmark on ePHPm, A/B tested the new in-process database bridge against the wire path, and started building ephpm/db-wordpress, a wpdb drop-in that talks to the database in-process instead of over a socket. Between them they produced six litewire issues in about three hours. None of them broke the install. All of them made WordPress quietly do the wrong thing.

item.title: Building a Custom SAPI - How PHP Actually Talks to the Outside World
item.description: If you’ve only ever run PHP behind nginx you’ve probably never had to think about how echo reaches a socket. When you embed PHP, as ePHPm does, it’s the first thing you have to answer, and the answer is a SAPI. There is very little written about implementing one. Most of what I know came from reading sapi/cli, sapi/cgi and sapi/embed in php-src and then finding out which parts I’d misread. This is the write-up I wanted back in March.

item.title: SQLite as a Production Database via Protocol Translation
item.description: Most of the PHP sites I’d put on ePHPm don’t need a MySQL server. A brochure WordPress, an internal Laravel tool, a preview environment that lives for an afternoon. What they do need is something that looks like MySQL, because mysqli and pdo_mysql are the only database drivers their code has ever been pointed at. I mentioned this in the ePHPm pragmatism post as a one-paragraph “because”. This is the longer version, now that WordPress 7.0 and Laravel 13 both install and run end to end on it.
